Hace veinte años, las empresas derribaro:
Hace veinte años, las empresas derribaron las paredes con una promesa: si todos compartíamos el mismo espacio, hablaríamos más, colaboraríamos mejor y las ideas circularían solas. Hoy, en muchas oficinas abiertas de Madrid o Barcelona, lo que más se oye es... nada. Decenas de personas trabajan en silencio, con los {auriculares|headphones} puestos, y se escriben por chat aunque estén sentadas a dos metros.

El hecho de que la gente se aísle no debería sorprendernos, explica la psicóloga laboral Marta Ibáñez. «Cuando no hay paredes, cada uno construye las suyas. Los auriculares son la puerta que la arquitectura nos quitó». Según varios estudios, en los espacios abiertos las conversaciones cara a cara no aumentan, sino que disminuyen, porque nadie quiere que todo el equipo escuche lo que dice.

Algunas empresas han empezado a {rectificar|change course}. En una consultora de Valencia han creado «zonas de biblioteca», donde está prohibido hablar, y salas pequeñas para llamadas. «Que la gente pueda elegir dónde trabaja según la tarea es lo que de verdad ha cambiado el ambiente», cuenta su directora. Otras, en cambio, han optado por el modelo híbrido: a la oficina se va a reunirse; a concentrarse, a casa.

Ibáñez, sin embargo, advierte de que el problema no es solo de espacio. «Comprendo que las empresas quieran ahorrar metros cuadrados, pero si no se respeta el tiempo de concentración, da igual que haya paredes o no». Su consejo es sencillo: acordar en equipo cuándo se puede interrumpir y cuándo no.
Vor zwanzig Jahren rissen die Firmen die:
Twenty years ago companies tore down the walls with a promise: if we all shared the same space, we'd talk more, work together better, and ideas would flow by themselves. Today, in many open-plan offices in Madrid or Barcelona, what you hear most is … nothing. Dozens of people work in silence, headphones on, and message each other on chat even though they're sitting two metres apart.

The fact that people cut themselves off shouldn't surprise us, explains occupational psychologist Marta Ibáñez. "When there are no walls, everyone builds their own. Headphones are the door that architecture took away from us." According to several studies, face-to-face conversations in open spaces don't increase but decrease, because nobody wants the whole team to hear what they're saying.

Some companies have started to change course. A consultancy in Valencia has created "library zones", where talking is forbidden, and small rooms for phone calls. "Letting people choose where they work depending on the task is what has really changed the atmosphere," says its director. Others, by contrast, have opted for the hybrid model: you go to the office to meet; to concentrate, you stay home.

Ibáñez warns, however, that the problem isn't just about space. "I understand that companies want to save square metres, but if concentration time isn't respected, it doesn't matter whether there are walls or not." Her advice is simple: agree as a team when interruptions are OK and when they're not.
Ein Comedian über Witze in der Fremdspra: A comedian on jokes in a foreign language
Tomás Achterberg nació en Utrecht, lleva:
Tomás Achterberg nació en Utrecht, lleva doce años en Sevilla y desde hace tres hace monólogos en bares y pequeños teatros. Hablamos con él antes de una actuación.

—¿Cómo se le ocurre a un holandés hacer humor en español?
—Pues metiendo la pata. Al principio me reía de mis propios errores: el día que le dije a mi suegra que estaba «embarazado» en vez de «avergonzado», por ejemplo. La gente se partía de risa y pensé: aquí hay material.

—¿Es más difícil hacer reír en otro idioma?
—Muchísimo. Puedes dominar la gramática y aun así no pillar un chiste. El humor depende del ritmo, de las referencias, de saber qué se puede decir y qué no. Eso no viene en ningún libro. Yo tardé años en entender por qué todo el mundo se reía cuando alguien decía «{¡que te den morcilla!|roughly: get lost!}».

—¿Cambia de registro según el público?
—Claro. En un bar de barrio puedo soltar un par de tacos y nadie se escandaliza; en un festival con familias, me corto un poco. Lo que nunca hago es reírme de la gente del público. Me río de mí mismo, que es más barato y no ofende a nadie.

—¿Algún consejo para quien aprende español?
—Que no se agobie si no entiende las bromas. Es normal. Yo digo que el humor es como el {acento|accent}: lo último que se aprende y lo primero que te delata. Y que se {atreva|dare} a equivocarse en voz alta, que de los errores salen los mejores chistes.
Tomás Achterberg wurde in Utrecht gebore:
Tomás Achterberg was born in Utrecht, has lived in Seville for twelve years and has been doing stand-up comedy in bars and small theatres for three. We talk to him before a show.

– How does a Dutchman come up with the idea of doing comedy in Spanish?
– By putting his foot in it. At first I laughed at my own mistakes: the day I told my mother-in-law I was "embarazado" (pregnant) instead of "avergonzado" (embarrassed), for example. People were in stitches and I thought: there's material here.

– Is it harder to make people laugh in another language?
– Much harder. You can master the grammar and still not get a joke. Humour depends on rhythm, on references, on knowing what you can and can't say. That isn't in any book. It took me years to understand why everyone laughed when someone said "¡que te den morcilla!".

– Do you change register depending on the audience?
– Of course. In a neighbourhood bar I can let slip a couple of swear words and nobody's shocked; at a festival with families I hold back a bit. What I never do is make fun of people in the audience. I laugh at myself – it's cheaper and doesn't offend anyone.

– Any advice for people learning Spanish?
– Don't get stressed if you don't understand the jokes. It's normal. I always say humour is like an accent: the last thing you learn and the first thing that gives you away. And dare to make mistakes out loud, because the best jokes come from mistakes.

Señor director:

Leo con interés que el Ayuntamiento pretende construir un nuevo carril bici en la avenida principal de nuestro barrio. Vaya por delante que soy ciclista: voy al trabajo en bici desde hace ocho años, llueva o haga sol. Precisamente por eso me permito hacer algunas observaciones.

Apoyaré el proyecto siempre que el carril esté separado físicamente del tráfico. Una simple línea pintada en el suelo no protege a nadie; solo sirve para que las autoridades puedan decir que «han hecho algo». Tampoco tengo nada en contra de que se eliminen plazas de aparcamiento, con tal de que se informe a los comerciantes con tiempo y se habiliten zonas de carga y descarga.

Lo que no entiendo es el trazado. Según los planos publicados, el carril se interrumpe dos veces y obliga a los ciclistas a cruzar una rotonda sin semáforo. A no ser que alguien me demuestre lo contrario, eso es una {invitación|invitation} al accidente. En caso de que el proyecto siga adelante tal y como está, me temo que muchos vecinos seguirán prefiriendo el coche, y con razón.

Por último, pido que se escuche a quienes usamos la bici a diario. De haber consultado a las asociaciones de ciclistas, el Ayuntamiento se habría ahorrado más de un error. No se trata de estar a favor o en contra de la bici, sino de hacer las cosas bien.

Atentamente,
Lucía Ferrer Molina (Zaragoza)

Dear Editor,

I read with interest that the City Council intends to build a new cycle lane on the main avenue of our neighbourhood. Let me say from the outset that I'm a cyclist: I've cycled to work for eight years, rain or shine. Precisely for that reason, I'd like to make a few observations.

I will support the project provided the lane is physically separated from the traffic. A simple line painted on the road protects no one; it only allows the authorities to say they've "done something". Nor do I have anything against parking spaces being removed, as long as shopkeepers are informed in good time and loading zones are provided.

What I don't understand is the route. According to the published plans, the lane is interrupted twice and forces cyclists to cross a roundabout without traffic lights. Unless someone can prove otherwise, that's an invitation to an accident. If the project goes ahead as it stands, I'm afraid many residents will keep preferring the car – and rightly so.

Finally, I ask that those of us who cycle every day be listened to. Had the Council consulted the cycling associations, it would have avoided more than one mistake. It's not about being for or against bikes, but about doing things properly.

Yours faithfully,
Lucía Ferrer Molina (Zaragoza)

Hay novelas que se leen de un tirón y otras que piden ir despacio. La segunda obra de la gallega Iria Castro, «La casa de las persianas bajadas», pertenece claramente al segundo grupo, y eso, lejos de ser un defecto, es su mayor virtud.

La historia es sencilla: tras la muerte de su madre, tres hermanos que llevan años sin hablarse vuelven a la casa familiar de Lugo para vaciarla. Durante una semana de lluvia, entre cajas, fotos y facturas antiguas, van saliendo a la luz los {rencores|grudges} de siempre y algún secreto que nadie esperaba. Lo interesante no es tanto lo que pasa como lo que no se dice: Castro construye la tensión a base de silencios, frases a medias y miradas que el lector tiene que interpretar.

Lo mejor del libro es, sin duda, el retrato de los personajes. Ninguno es del todo bueno ni del todo malo; los tres resultan tan {entrañables|endearing} como irritantes, igual que los hermanos de verdad. Ahora bien, la novela no está exenta de problemas. El ritmo del tercio central decae, y algunos capítulos dedicados a la infancia de la madre, aunque bien escritos, parecen pertenecer a otro libro.

En lo que respecta al estilo, Castro escribe con una prosa limpia, sin adornos innecesarios, en la que de vez en cuando se cuela alguna palabra en gallego que da color al conjunto. Dicho esto, quien busque giros {argumentales|plot} espectaculares saldrá decepcionado.

En resumen: una novela sobria y honesta sobre lo difícil que es hablar con quienes más queremos. No es para todos los públicos, pero quien tenga paciencia encontrará en ella mucho más de lo que promete su discreta portada.
Es gibt Romane, die man in einem Zug lie:
Some novels you read in one sitting, others ask you to take your time. The second work by Galician author Iria Castro, "The House with the Shutters Down", clearly belongs to the second group – and far from being a flaw, that's its greatest strength.

The story is simple: after their mother's death, three siblings who haven't spoken for years return to the family home in Lugo to clear it out. Over a rainy week, among boxes, photos and old bills, the old grudges come to light, along with a secret nobody expected. What's interesting isn't so much what happens as what isn't said: Castro builds tension out of silences, half-finished sentences and looks the reader has to interpret.

The best thing about the book is undoubtedly its portrayal of the characters. None is entirely good or entirely bad; all three are as endearing as they are irritating, just like real siblings. That said, the novel isn't without its problems. The pace drops in the middle third, and some chapters about the mother's childhood, though well written, seem to belong to a different book.

As for style, Castro writes clean prose without unnecessary embellishment, into which the occasional Galician word slips, adding colour to the whole. Having said that, anyone looking for spectacular plot twists will be disappointed.

In short: a sober, honest novel about how hard it is to talk to the people we love most. It's not for everyone, but those with patience will find in it much more than its modest cover promises.

Quería yo dedicar esta columna a un inve:
Quería yo dedicar esta columna a un invento injustamente {denostado|reviled}: la reunión. Se la acusa de robar tiempo, de no servir para nada y de haber podido ser un correo electrónico. Calumnias. Quien así habla no ha sabido apreciar sus muchas virtudes.

Pensemos, sin ir más lejos, en la reunión de los lunes a las nueve. ¿Qué otra actividad permite a doce personas descubrir, al mismo tiempo y en directo, que nadie ha leído el documento adjunto? Ninguna. Y, sin embargo, ahí estamos todos, asintiendo con gravedad, como si el {orden del día|agenda} fuera un texto sagrado.

Admiremos también la creatividad lingüística que florece en estas citas. Solo en una reunión se puede «poner en valor», «bajar a tierra» y «tener una visión de trescientos sesenta grados» antes del primer café. Solo en una reunión «lo vemos» significa «no lo haremos nunca» y «buena pregunta» quiere decir «no tengo ni idea».

Pero su mayor mérito es otro: la reunión nos enseña humildad. Uno llega convencido de que su trabajo es urgente y sale, dos horas después, comprendiendo que lo verdaderamente urgente era convocar otra reunión para la semana que viene. ¿Será posible mayor lección de {desapego|detachment, letting go}?

Por eso propongo que se declare la reunión patrimonio inmaterial de la humanidad. Eso sí, que alguien convoque antes una reunión para decidir quién redacta la propuesta. Yo, lamentablemente, no podré asistir: tengo otra a la misma hora.
Ich wollte diese Kolumne einer zu Unrech:
I wanted to devote this column to an unjustly reviled invention: the meeting. It's accused of stealing time, of being useless and of something that could have been an email. Slander! Whoever says that hasn't learnt to appreciate its many virtues.

Think, for instance, of the Monday meeting at nine. What other activity allows twelve people to discover, at the same time and live, that nobody has read the attached document? None. And yet there we all are, nodding gravely, as if the agenda were a sacred text.

Let us also admire the linguistic creativity that blossoms at these gatherings. Only in a meeting can you "leverage value", "bring it down to earth" and "take a 360-degree view" before your first coffee. Only in a meeting does "we'll look into it" mean "we'll never do it", and "good question" mean "I have no idea".

But its greatest merit is something else: the meeting teaches us humility. You walk in convinced your work is urgent and walk out, two hours later, realising that what was truly urgent was to call another meeting for next week. Could there be a greater lesson in detachment?

That's why I propose that the meeting be declared intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Mind you, someone should first call a meeting to decide who drafts the proposal. Unfortunately, I won't be able to attend: I have another one at the same time.

– Welcome to "Science at the Table". Today we're talking about a topic that, incidentally, follows us Spaniards wherever we go: the siesta. With me is sleep researcher Carmen Lozano. Carmen, is it true that everyone in Spain has a siesta?
– Far from it. It's one of those clichés that get repeated ad nauseam. Surveys show that only a minority have one every day, mainly pensioners and shift workers. Most people, during the week, have neither the time nor a place to lie down for a bit.
– So we've been stuck with a label.
– Exactly. That said, it doesn't change the fact that the siesta has a biological basis. After lunch – and not just because of the food – our internal clock causes a natural dip in attention. It happens everywhere; it's just that in other countries people push through with coffee.
– And is it good or bad for your health?
– It depends on how you do it. A short nap, twenty minutes at most, improves memory and mood. If you go beyond half an hour, you enter deep sleep and wake up feeling wrecked, worse than before. Not to mention that you then find it hard to fall asleep at night.
– So the famous "pyjamas-and-chamber-pot siesta" …
– … is a bad idea, however much we like the name. My advice: short, early in the afternoon and, if possible, without feeling guilty. Better a nap in time than a whole afternoon of yawning.
Dicen en el pueblo que el viejo Anselmo:
Dicen en el pueblo que el viejo Anselmo subió al faro la noche en que se fue la luz en toda la costa, y que no volvió a bajar hasta el amanecer. Nadie le había pedido nada; hacía veinte años que el faro funcionaba solo, gobernado por una máquina que alguien vigilaba desde una oficina en La Coruña.

Aquella noche, sin embargo, la máquina calló. El mar golpeaba las rocas con una rabia antigua y, a lo lejos, un pesquero buscaba el puerto a ciegas. Anselmo, que había sido farero durante cuarenta años, no lo dudó. Cogió el {farol|lantern} de aceite que guardaba en el desván, subió los ciento doce peldaños que se sabía de memoria y, con las manos temblorosas, encendió la vieja lámpara de reserva.

Quien hubiere visto aquella luz desde el mar —escribiría después el patrón del pesquero en una carta al periódico— no la habría confundido con ninguna otra. Era débil, irregular, casi humana. Pero bastó.

Al día siguiente, los técnicos de la capital llegaron con sus coches y sus informes. Revisaron cables, culparon a la tormenta y se marcharon sin preguntar quién había encendido la lámpara. Anselmo tampoco se lo contó a nadie. Sea como fuere, desde entonces los pescadores, al pasar frente al cabo, levantan la mano hacia la torre, por si acaso alguien sigue allí arriba, velando.

Dondequiera que vayan los barcos del pueblo, dicen, llevan consigo un poco de aquella luz.
Im Dorf erzählt man, dass der alte Ansel:
They say in the village that old Anselmo climbed the lighthouse on the night the power went out along the whole coast, and didn't come down again until dawn. Nobody had asked him to; for twenty years the lighthouse had run by itself, controlled by a machine that someone monitored from an office in A Coruña.

That night, however, the machine fell silent. The sea struck the rocks with an ancient rage and, in the distance, a fishing boat was searching blindly for the harbour. Anselmo, who had been the lighthouse keeper for forty years, didn't hesitate. He took the oil lantern he kept in the attic, climbed the hundred and twelve steps he knew by heart and, with trembling hands, lit the old reserve lamp.

Whoever might have seen that light from the sea – the skipper of the fishing boat would later write in a letter to the newspaper – would not have mistaken it for any other. It was weak, irregular, almost human. But it was enough.

The next day the technicians from the capital arrived with their cars and their reports. They checked cables, blamed the storm and left without asking who had lit the lamp. Anselmo didn't tell anyone either. Be that as it may, ever since then the fishermen, as they pass the cape, raise a hand towards the tower, just in case someone is still up there, keeping watch.

Wherever the village boats go, they say, they carry a little of that light with them.

Solemos pensar en el olvido como en un fallo: la memoria sería un archivo y olvidar, perder documentos. La neurociencia actual propone una imagen bien distinta. Olvidar, dicho de otro modo, no es un error del sistema, sino una de sus funciones.

Ya a finales del siglo XIX, el psicólogo alemán Hermann Ebbinghaus se aprendió de memoria listas de sílabas sin sentido y midió cuánto recordaba con el paso del tiempo. El resultado, conocido como «curva del olvido», es tan sencillo como {demoledor|devastating}: la mayor parte de lo aprendido se pierde en las primeras horas y días, a no ser que se repase.

Ahora bien, Ebbinghaus descubrió también la otra cara de la moneda. Cada vez que repasaba una lista justo cuando estaba a punto de olvidarla, la curva se volvía más plana; o lo que es lo mismo, el recuerdo duraba más. En ese principio se basan hoy las aplicaciones de repaso espaciado: no se trata de repetir mucho, sino de repetir en el momento oportuno.

¿Y por qué olvida el cerebro con tanta facilidad? Porque recordarlo todo sería, paradójicamente, un estorbo. Un cerebro que guardara cada detalle —cada número de teléfono, cada conversación banal— tendría muchas más dificultades para quedarse con lo importante y para {generalizar|generalise}. El olvido actúa como un filtro: descarta lo que no usamos para dejar sitio a lo que sí.

En suma, quien aprende un idioma no debería desesperarse cuando una palabra se le escapa. Mejor dicho: debería alegrarse. Ese pequeño esfuerzo por recuperarla es, precisamente, lo que hará que la próxima vez se quede.
Wir stellen uns das Vergessen meist als:
We tend to think of forgetting as a failure: memory would be an archive, and forgetting would mean losing documents. Today's neuroscience suggests a very different picture. Forgetting, in other words, isn't a system error but one of its functions.

As early as the late 19th century, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables and measured how much he remembered over time. The result, known as the "forgetting curve", is as simple as it is devastating: most of what we learn is lost in the first hours and days, unless it's reviewed.

However, Ebbinghaus also discovered the other side of the coin. Each time he reviewed a list just as he was about to forget it, the curve became flatter; or, to put it another way, the memory lasted longer. Today's spaced-repetition apps are based on this principle: it's not about repeating a lot, but about repeating at the right moment.

And why does the brain forget so easily? Because remembering everything would, paradoxically, be a hindrance. A brain that stored every detail – every phone number, every trivial conversation – would find it much harder to hold on to what matters and to generalise. Forgetting acts as a filter: it discards what we don't use to make room for what we do.

In short, anyone learning a language shouldn't despair when a word slips their mind. Better still: they should be glad. That small effort to retrieve it is precisely what will make it stick next time.

El sábado quiero ir a la playa de la Barceloneta. Tomo el metro en Fontana, la línea verde. Pero no {cambio|I change} de línea en Passeig de Gràcia y llego a... ¡Zona Universitaria! Estoy muy lejos de la playa.

Pregunto a una señora: —Perdone, ¿sabe dónde está la playa? —¡Uy, está muy lejos! —dice ella—. Tome la línea verde otra vez y cambie a la línea amarilla en Passeig de Gràcia. Baje en Barceloneta. Después siga todo recto unos diez minutos.

Una hora después estoy en la playa. Hace sol, hay mucha gente y el mar es azul. —Bueno —pienso—, ahora conozco muy bien el metro de Barcelona.
Am Samstag will ich an den Strand von Ba:
On Saturday I want to go to Barceloneta beach. I take the metro at Fontana, the green line. But I don't change lines at Passeig de Gràcia and I end up at … Zona Universitaria! I'm very far from the beach.

I ask a lady: “Excuse me, do you know where the beach is?” “Oh, it's very far!” she says. “Take the green line again and change to the yellow line at Passeig de Gràcia. Get off at Barceloneta. Then go straight on for about ten minutes.”

An hour later I'm at the beach. It's sunny, there are lots of people and the sea is blue. “Well,” I think, “now I know the Barcelona metro really well.”
Este fin de semana Laia y yo hemos ido a:
Este fin de semana Laia y yo hemos ido a Sitges, un pueblo en la costa, a cuarenta minutos de Barcelona en tren. ¡Ha sido genial!

Hemos llegado el sábado por la mañana. Primero hemos paseado por el casco antiguo, con sus casas blancas y sus calles {estrechas|narrow}. Después hemos comido una paella en un restaurante al lado del mar. Por la tarde hemos nadado un poco, aunque el agua estaba fría.

Laia me ha preguntado: —¿Has estado alguna vez en un pueblo así? —No, nunca —he dicho yo—. En Hamburgo también hay mar, pero no hay palmeras. Hemos vuelto a casa muy tarde y muy cansados, pero muy {contentos|happy}.
Dieses Wochenende sind Laia und ich nach:
This weekend Laia and I went to Sitges, a town on the coast, forty minutes from Barcelona by train. It was great!

We arrived on Saturday morning. First we walked around the old town, with its white houses and narrow streets. Then we had paella in a restaurant by the sea. In the afternoon we swam a bit, although the water was cold.

Laia asked me: “Have you ever been to a town like this?” “No, never,” I said. “There's sea in Hamburg too, but no palm trees.” We got home very late and very tired, but very happy.
Normalmente me levanto a las siete y med:
Normalmente me levanto a las siete y media. Me ducho, me visto y desayuno un café con leche y una tostada. A las nueve tengo clase en la universidad. Mi compañero Marc siempre llega tarde: es más simpático que yo, pero menos {puntual|punctual}.

Pero hoy no es un día normal. Hoy me he despertado a las nueve menos cuarto. ¡La alarma no ha {sonado|gone off}! Me he vestido en dos minutos, no he desayunado y he corrido al metro.

Cuando he llegado a clase, el profesor estaba explicando algo en la pizarra. Marc me ha mirado y ha dicho en voz baja: —Hoy tú eres el que llega tarde. ¡Por fin no soy el único!
Normalerweise stehe ich um halb acht auf:
I usually get up at half past seven. I have a shower, get dressed and have a milky coffee and toast for breakfast. At nine I have class at university. My classmate Marc always arrives late: he's nicer than me, but less punctual.

But today isn't a normal day. Today I woke up at quarter to nine. The alarm didn't go off! I got dressed in two minutes, didn't have breakfast and ran to the metro.

When I got to class, the teacher was explaining something on the board. Marc looked at me and said quietly: “Today you're the one who's late. At last I'm not the only one!”
El jueves es {festivo|Feiertag} y muchos:
El jueves es {festivo|a public holiday} y muchos catalanes hacen «puente»: no trabajan el viernes y tienen cuatro días libres. Nuria va a visitar a su familia en Valencia. Pablo va a ir a un festival de música. ¿Y yo?

—¿Qué vas a hacer tú? —me pregunta Laia. —No sé. ¿Tienes ganas de ir a los Pirineos? —¡Me encanta la idea! Pero mira el tiempo: el jueves va a llover y va a hacer frío. —Pues {llevamos|we take} chaquetas y botas —digo yo.

Al final vamos a ir a Puigcerdà, un pueblo en la montaña. Vamos a hacer {senderismo|hiking} el viernes y el sábado. El domingo, si hace buen tiempo, vamos a volver por la costa. —¡Va a ser un puente perfecto! —dice Laia.
Am Donnerstag ist Feiertag und viele Kat:
Thursday is a public holiday and many Catalans make a “bridge”: they don't work on Friday and have four days off. Nuria is going to visit her family in Valencia. Pablo is going to a music festival. And me?

“What are you going to do?” Laia asks me. “I don't know. Do you fancy going to the Pyrenees?” “I love the idea! But look at the weather: on Thursday it's going to rain and be cold.” “Then we'll take jackets and boots,” I say.

In the end we're going to Puigcerdà, a village in the mountains. We're going hiking on Friday and Saturday. On Sunday, if the weather's good, we're going to come back along the coast. “It's going to be a perfect long weekend!” says Laia.
El domingo Nuria y yo visitamos al señor:
El domingo Nuria y yo visitamos al señor Puig, nuestro {casero|landlord}. Tiene ochenta años y vive en el primer piso. Nos invita a un café y nos enseña fotos antiguas.

—Cuando yo era joven, Gràcia era muy diferente —dice—. No había tantos turistas. Todos los vecinos se conocían. Los niños jugaban en la calle y las {abuelas|grandmothers} se sentaban delante de las puertas por la tarde. Mi padre tenía una pequeña tienda de {zapatos|shoes} en esta calle.

—¿Y qué hacían los jóvenes los fines de semana? —pregunto yo. —Íbamos a bailar a la plaza del Sol. No teníamos móviles, así que quedábamos siempre a la misma hora en el mismo lugar. ¡Y nadie llegaba tarde! —dice, y se ríe.
Am Sonntag besuchen Nuria und ich Herrn:
On Sunday Nuria and I visit Mr Puig, our landlord. He's eighty and lives on the first floor. He invites us for a coffee and shows us old photos.

“When I was young, Gràcia was very different,” he says. “There weren't so many tourists. All the neighbours knew each other. The children played in the street and the grandmothers sat in front of their doors in the afternoon. My father had a small shoe shop in this street.”

“And what did young people do at the weekend?” I ask. “We used to go dancing in the Plaza del Sol. We didn't have mobile phones, so we always met at the same time in the same place. And nobody was ever late!” he says, and laughs.
Antes los vecinos no se conocían.
Marc buscaba unas prácticas desde hacía:
Marc buscaba unas prácticas desde hacía meses. La semana pasada por fin lo llamaron de una empresa de tecnología en el 22@, el barrio de las {startups|start-ups}.

El día de la entrevista se levantó a las seis, se puso su mejor camisa y repasó su currículum tres veces. Llegó media hora antes. La entrevistadora era muy amable. Le preguntó por sus estudios, por sus puntos fuertes y por qué quería trabajar allí. Marc contestó con calma, aunque estaba muy nervioso.

Al final ella le preguntó: —¿Habla usted otros idiomas? —Catalán, castellano, inglés... y estoy aprendiendo alemán con un amigo —dijo Marc. Ella sonrió. Dos días después lo llamaron otra vez: ¡consiguió el puesto! Esa noche lo celebramos en el bar de siempre.
Marc had been looking for an internship for months. Last week a technology company in 22@, the start-up district, finally called him.

On the day of the interview he got up at six, put on his best shirt and went over his CV three times. He arrived half an hour early. The interviewer was very friendly. She asked him about his studies, his strengths and why he wanted to work there. Marc answered calmly, although he was very nervous.

At the end she asked him: “Do you speak other languages?” “Catalan, Spanish, English … and I'm learning German with a friend,” said Marc. She smiled. Two days later they called him again: he got the job! That evening we celebrated at our usual bar.
La Mercè es la gran fiesta de Barcelona,:
La Mercè es la gran fiesta de Barcelona, en septiembre. Hay conciertos, {castellers|human towers} y el «correfoc», con fuego y música por las calles. Yo tenía muchas ganas de verlo todo.

Pero el viernes me desperté con fiebre. Me dolía la cabeza y la garganta. Nuria me miró y dijo: —Tienes muy mala cara. Quédate en la cama, bebe mucha agua y toma un ibuprofeno. Y no salgas esta noche. —¡Pero es el correfoc! —dije yo. —El año que viene hay otro —contestó ella.

Nuria fue a la farmacia y me trajo un jarabe y una sopa de su madre. El domingo ya me encontraba mejor y pude ver los castellers en la plaza Sant Jaume. Eran increíbles: ¡nueve {pisos|storeys} de personas!
Die Mercè ist das große Fest von Barcelo:
La Mercè is Barcelona's big festival, in September. There are concerts, human towers and the “correfoc”, with fire and music through the streets. I was really looking forward to seeing it all.

But on Friday I woke up with a temperature. My head and throat hurt. Nuria looked at me and said: “You look awful. Stay in bed, drink lots of water and take an ibuprofen. And don't go out tonight.” “But it's the correfoc!” I said. “There'll be another one next year,” she replied.

Nuria went to the pharmacy and brought me cough syrup and some soup from her mother. By Sunday I was already feeling better and I could see the human towers in the Plaça Sant Jaume. They were incredible: nine storeys of people!
Los castellers tenían ___ pisos de perso: Los castellers tenían ___ pisos de personas.
Mañana llega mi amigo Lukas desde Mannhe:
Mañana llega mi amigo Lukas desde Mannheim y quiero que todo sea perfecto. Le he escrito una lista de consejos: «Te recomiendo que traigas ropa ligera, pero también una chaqueta. Es importante que compres una tarjeta de transporte en el aeropuerto. Y no dejes la mochila sola en la playa».

Nuria se ríe cuando ve la lista. —Pareces su madre —me dice—. Déjale que descubra la ciudad solo. —Ya, pero quiero que le guste Barcelona tanto como a mí —contesto.

Miro el {pronóstico|forecast} del tiempo: dicen que el sábado puede llover. Ojalá no llueva, porque quiero que subamos al {búnker|bunker} del Carmel para ver la puesta de sol. Nuria me da una {palmada|pat} en el hombro: —Tranquilo. Si llueve, os llevo a comer el mejor arroz de la ciudad. Espero que tenga hambre.
Morgen kommt mein Freund Lukas aus Mannh:
Tomorrow my friend Lukas arrives from Mannheim and I want everything to be perfect. I've written him a list of tips: “I recommend you bring light clothes, but also a jacket. It's important that you buy a travel card at the airport. And don't leave your backpack alone on the beach.”

Nuria laughs when she sees the list. “You sound like his mother,” she says. “Let him discover the city on his own.” “I know, but I want him to like Barcelona as much as I do,” I reply.

I check the weather forecast: they say it might rain on Saturday. Hopefully it won't, because I want us to go up to the Carmel bunker to watch the sunset. Nuria pats me on the shoulder: “Relax. If it rains, I'll take you to eat the best rice in the city. I hope he's hungry.”
Era un martes de noviembre y llovía much:
Era un martes de noviembre y llovía mucho. Nuria estaba cocinando, Pablo veía una serie y yo estaba escribiendo un trabajo para la universidad. De repente, se fue la luz en todo el barrio.

Al principio nadie dijo nada. Luego Pablo gritó desde el sofá: —¡Justo en el último capítulo! Yo estaba peor: no había guardado mi trabajo desde hacía dos horas. Nuria encontró unas {velas|candles} en la cocina y las encendimos.

Como no podíamos hacer nada, nos sentamos los tres en el suelo del salón y empezamos a contar historias. Pablo nos contó que de pequeño se había perdido en la Feria de Abril de Sevilla. Nuria nos contó cómo había conocido a su mejor amiga. Cuando volvió la luz, a las once, nos dimos cuenta de que habíamos estado hablando tres horas. —Deberíamos apagar la luz más a menudo —dijo Nuria. Y, por suerte, mi ordenador había guardado el trabajo {automáticamente|automatically}.
Es war ein Dienstag im November und es r:
It was a Tuesday in November and it was raining hard. Nuria was cooking, Pablo was watching a series and I was writing an essay for university. Suddenly the power went out in the whole neighbourhood.

At first nobody said anything. Then Pablo shouted from the sofa: “Right in the last episode!” I was worse off: I hadn't saved my essay for two hours. Nuria found some candles in the kitchen and we lit them.

As we couldn't do anything, the three of us sat on the living-room floor and started telling stories. Pablo told us that as a child he had got lost at the Feria de Abril in Seville. Nuria told us how she had met her best friend. When the power came back at eleven, we realised we had been talking for three hours. “We should turn the lights off more often,” said Nuria. And luckily my computer had saved the essay automatically.
El lunes recibí un correo de una empresa:
El lunes recibí un correo de una empresa de Múnich. Me ofrecían un trabajo fijo, con un sueldo que en Barcelona solo podría soñar. Aunque llevaba meses buscando algo así, no me alegré tanto como esperaba. Me quedé mirando la pantalla un buen rato.

Esa noche se lo conté a Nuria y a Laia en la terraza. —Si yo fuera tú, lo aceptaría sin pensarlo —dijo Nuria—. Con ese sueldo podrías ahorrar y volver cuando quisieras. Laia, en cambio, no dijo nada durante un rato. Luego me miró y me preguntó: —¿Y tú qué quieres? No lo que deberías querer, sino lo que quieres de verdad.

No supe qué contestar. Como no podía dormir, salí a pasear por Gràcia. Se oían risas en las plazas y alguien tocaba la guitarra. Pensé en mi primer día, cuando no entendía nada y me perdí en el metro. Si alguien me hubiera dicho entonces que algún día me costaría tanto irme, no lo habría creído.

Al día siguiente escribí a la empresa. Les agradecí la oferta y les pregunté si sería posible trabajar en remoto desde Barcelona. Me contestaron que lo {estudiarían|would look into it}. Todavía no sé qué pasará, pero por primera vez tengo claro lo que quiero.
Am Montag bekam ich eine E-Mail von eine:
On Monday I got an email from a company in Munich. They were offering me a permanent job, with a salary I could only dream of in Barcelona. Although I'd been looking for something like that for months, I wasn't as happy as I'd expected. I sat staring at the screen for quite a while.

That evening I told Nuria and Laia about it on the terrace. "If I were you, I'd accept it without thinking twice," said Nuria. "With that salary you could save and come back whenever you wanted." Laia, on the other hand, said nothing for a while. Then she looked at me and asked: "And what do you want? Not what you should want, but what you really want."

I didn't know what to answer. As I couldn't sleep, I went for a walk around Gràcia. You could hear laughter in the squares and someone was playing the guitar. I thought about my first day, when I didn't understand anything and got lost in the metro. If someone had told me then that one day I'd find it so hard to leave, I wouldn't have believed it.

The next day I wrote to the company. I thanked them for the offer and asked if it would be possible to work remotely from Barcelona. They replied that they would look into it. I still don't know what will happen, but for the first time I'm clear about what I want.
Fue un martes lluvioso cuando Laia me ll:
Fue un martes lluvioso cuando Laia me llamó desde el archivo de la Biblioteca de Catalunya, donde hacía prácticas. —Tienes que venir. No te imaginas lo que he encontrado —me dijo, en voz tan baja que apenas la oí.

Lo que había encontrado era un cuaderno escrito a mano, metido por error en una caja de facturas de 1936. Por muy acostumbrada que estuviera a los documentos antiguos, a Laia le temblaban las manos. Las primeras páginas eran recetas de cocina; ahora bien, a partir de la página veinte, la letra cambiaba y empezaba un diario. Era de una chica de diecisiete años, Mercè, que vivía en Gràcia, a dos calles de nuestro piso.

Pasamos la tarde leyéndolo. Mercè hablaba de los bombardeos con una calma que daba miedo, y eso que, a veces, describía cómo se escondían en el metro. Lo que más me conmovió, sin embargo, no fueron las escenas de guerra, sino lo normal que intentaba ser su vida: los nervios antes de un baile, una pelea con su hermana, un chico que le gustaba.

—Si no lo hubiera abierto por curiosidad, se habría quedado ahí otros noventa años —dijo Laia. De ahí que, a la semana siguiente, la biblioteca decidiera revisar todas las cajas de esa época. Y fue así como, buscando una vida, encontraron cientos.
Es war an einem regnerischen Dienstag, a:
It was a rainy Tuesday when Laia called me from the archive of the Biblioteca de Catalunya, where she was doing an internship. "You have to come. You can't imagine what I've found," she said, so quietly that I could barely hear her.

What she had found was a handwritten notebook, put by mistake into a box of invoices from 1936. However used she was to old documents, Laia's hands were shaking. The first pages were recipes; from page twenty, however, the handwriting changed and a diary began. It belonged to a seventeen-year-old girl, Mercè, who lived in Gràcia, two streets from our flat.

We spent the afternoon reading it. Mercè wrote about the bombings with a calm that was frightening, even though she sometimes described how they hid in the metro. What moved me most, however, wasn't the war scenes, but how normal she tried to keep her life: the nerves before a dance, a fight with her sister, a boy she liked.

"If I hadn't opened it out of curiosity, it would have stayed there for another ninety years," said Laia. That's why, the following week, the library decided to go through all the boxes from that period. And that's how, looking for one life, they found hundreds.
Vor einem Jahr, um diese Zeit, landete i:
A year ago, around this time, I landed at El Prat with two suitcases and textbook Spanish. Today I'm writing from the same terrace in Gràcia where Nuria taught me to peel prawns without making a mess – which, incidentally, I still haven't mastered.

In the end, the company in Munich agreed to let me work remotely. I could hardly believe it myself: had I known, I'd have spared myself a few sleepless nights. Whatever happens with the contract next year, I have no more doubts about where I want to be. Laia says I've become "more Mediterranean than the sea"; Pablo, who's still in Madrid, says I've become "a real pain at after-dinner chats". However much they exaggerate, they have a point.

What has changed most, though, isn't where I live, but how I listen. I used to get stressed if I didn't understand a word; now I pay attention to what isn't said: Mrs Rovira's sharp undertone, the "we'll see" that really means "no", the "shall we meet up?" that never comes with a time. In other words: I've learnt the language that lies between the words.

Tonight is the Verbena de Sant Joan. Nuria's grandfather has promised to bring coca and proverbs in equal measure. "Better late than never," he said to me yesterday when I finally gave the neighbour her salt back. He's right. And if someone had told me a year ago that I'd end up quoting proverbs on a roof terrace in Barcelona, I'd have said they were pulling my leg.

2. If it ends in any other consonant → stress on the last syllable: hablar · ciudad · español

Words stressed on the third-to-last syllable always have an accent: teléfono · rápido · miércoles · América.

Accents distinguish words: tú (you) / tu (your) · él (he) / el (the) · sí (yes) / si (if) · mí / mi · más / mas. Question words always have an accent: qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo.

<p>Nimm die <b>3. Person Plural Indefini:
Take the 3rd person plural preterite, remove -ron and add -ra:

Preterite→ stemImperf. subj.

At first I didn't dare say anything. It was normal for interns to stay longer, a colleague explained to me. However, after three months I asked my boss if we could talk about it. To my surprise, she listened carefully and suggested we try the continuous working day in summer. It was the first time I felt my opinion counted. I learnt that sometimes it's better to speak up than to wait for things to change by themselves.

Ten years ago I missed a flight to London. I was about to start an internship at an advertising agency and, if I'd arrived on time, I'd probably be living there now. But the traffic jam that morning changed everything.

While I was waiting for the next flight, I met an older woman who was going back to Valencia. She told me about her language school and that she was looking for teachers. "If you're interested, call me," she said. I didn't think about it for long. Three months later, instead of designing ads in London, I was teaching English in Valencia.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I hadn't missed that flight. Maybe I'd have been successful in advertising, or maybe I'd have come back after six months. When I met Raquel at university, she was the shyest person in the class. She went red every time the lecturer asked her a question and never spoke in group discussions. Nobody would have said that ten years later she'd become one of the best-known journalists on the radio.

The change didn't happen overnight. She started working as an intern at a local station, where she had to do interviews in the street. "At first I was about to quit every week," she told me. The funny thing is that, in private, she's still quite shy. "On the radio I put on a different skin," she says, laughing. I was speechless the first time I heard her. And although we rarely see each other, whenever we meet we end up talking until all hours, like in the old days.

En los últimos años, varias empresas esp:
En los últimos años, varias empresas españolas han probado la semana laboral de cuatro días. Los resultados, según sus defensores, son {prometedores|promising}: los empleados están menos estresados y, sin embargo, producen lo mismo o incluso más.

No obstante, no todo el mundo está convencido. En primer lugar, no todos los sectores pueden reducir las horas: un hospital o un restaurante, por ejemplo, necesitan personal todos los días. En segundo lugar, hay quien teme que la jornada de los cuatro días restantes se vuelva más intensa, es decir, que se trabaje lo mismo en menos tiempo. Por otra parte, las pequeñas empresas dicen que no podrían permitírselo.

Cabe destacar, en cambio, que en los países donde se ha probado, como Islandia, la mayoría de las empresas acabaron manteniendo el modelo. En definitiva, la semana de cuatro días no es una solución mágica, pero quizá sí sea el principio de una nueva forma de entender el trabajo.
In den letzten Jahren haben mehrere span:
In recent years several Spanish companies have tried out the four-day working week. According to its supporters the results are promising: employees are less stressed and yet produce the same or even more.

Nevertheless, not everyone is convinced. Firstly, not all sectors can reduce their hours: a hospital or a restaurant, for example, needs staff every day. Secondly, some fear that the working day on the remaining four days will become more intense, that is, that people will do the same amount of work in less time. Furthermore, small businesses say they couldn't afford it.

It's worth pointing out, on the other hand, that in the countries where it has been tried, such as Iceland, most companies ended up keeping the model. All in all, the four-day week isn't a magic solution, but it may well be the beginning of a new way of thinking about work.

Los lingüistas calculan que buena parte:
Los lingüistas calculan que buena parte de lo que comunicamos no está en las palabras, sino en cómo y cuándo las decimos. Que alguien tarde en contestar un mensaje, por ejemplo, puede interpretarse como desinterés, aunque la razón sea simplemente que estaba conduciendo.

El hecho de que cada vez nos comuniquemos más por escrito ha multiplicado los malentendidos. En una conversación cara a cara, notamos enseguida si el otro está bromeando; en un chat, en cambio, un simple «vale» puede sonar frío o enfadado. Por eso hay quien sostiene que los emojis no son una moda infantil, sino una forma de {recuperar|win back} el tono que la escritura nos quita.

A mi entender, el problema no es la tecnología, sino que olvidamos ponernos en el lugar del otro. Que alguien nos responda con una sola palabra no significa necesariamente que esté molesto. Quizá, antes de sentirnos dolidos, deberíamos preguntar.
Linguisten schätzen, dass ein großer Tei:
Linguists estimate that a large part of what we communicate isn't in the words, but in how and when we say them. If someone takes a long time to reply to a message, for example, it can be interpreted as a lack of interest, even if the reason is simply that they were driving.

The fact that we communicate more and more in writing has multiplied misunderstandings. In a face-to-face conversation we notice straight away if the other person is joking; in a chat, on the other hand, a simple "OK" can sound cold or angry. That's why some argue that emojis aren't a childish fad but a way of winning back the tone that writing takes away from us.

In my view, the problem isn't technology, but that we forget to put ourselves in the other person's shoes. If someone answers us with a single word, it doesn't necessarily mean they're annoyed. Perhaps, before feeling hurt, we should ask.

Cuando llegué a Barcelona, había estudia:
Cuando llegué a Barcelona, había estudiado un español «de manual» y pensaba que lo entendería todo. Error. En la universidad, mis compañeros mezclaban castellano y catalán en la misma frase: «Ens veiem luego, ¿vale?». En la radio, un locutor andaluz se comía la mitad de las {consonantes|consonants}, y mi compañera de piso, que es de Sevilla, decía «quillo» cada dos por tres.

Luego conocí a una argentina que usaba «vos» en lugar de «tú» y a un mexicano para quien «coger» el autobús sonaba fatal. Tardé meses en entender que no hay un español correcto y otros incorrectos, sino muchas variedades igual de válidas. Lo que sí hay son registros: no hablamos igual con un amigo en el bar que con un profesor en una tutoría.

Hoy, más que «hablar bien», intento hablar de forma adecuada: saber cuándo puedo decir «tío, qué guay» y cuándo es mejor un «me parece estupendo». Y, dicho sea de paso, ya no me pierdo cuando alguien me dice «quillo».
Als ich nach Barcelona kam, hatte ich ei:
When I arrived in Barcelona, I had learnt "textbook" Spanish and thought I'd understand everything. Wrong. At university my fellow students mixed Spanish and Catalan in the same sentence: "Ens veiem luego, ¿vale?". On the radio, an Andalusian presenter swallowed half his consonants, and my flatmate, who is from Seville, said "quillo" every five minutes.

Then I met an Argentinian woman who used "vos" instead of "tú" and a Mexican man for whom "coger" the bus sounded terrible. It took me months to understand that there isn't one correct Spanish and other incorrect ones, but many equally valid varieties. What there are, though, are registers: we don't speak to a friend in a bar the same way we speak to a lecturer in office hours.

Today, rather than trying to "speak well", I try to speak appropriately: knowing when I can say "tío, qué guay" and when "me parece estupendo" is better. And, incidentally, I no longer get lost when someone calls me "quillo".

Lo primero que hacen la mayoría de los turistas en Barcelona es visitar la Sagrada Familia. Lo que pocos saben es que el modernismo catalán no fue obra de un solo genio. Fue un movimiento entero el que transformó la ciudad entre 1888 y 1911, y fueron arquitectos como Domènech i Montaner o Puig i Cadafalch quienes dejaron algunas de sus joyas más impresionantes.

El Palau de la Música Catalana, por ejemplo, es probablemente el edificio donde mejor se aprecia lo que pretendía el modernismo: unir arquitectura, escultura, vidrio y cerámica en una sola obra. Quien entra por primera vez no se imagina lo luminosa que es la sala, gracias a una enorme {claraboya|skylight} de cristal de colores.

Lo curioso es que durante décadas estos edificios se consideraron «de mal gusto». Fue a partir de los años setenta cuando se empezaron a valorar de nuevo. Hoy, en cambio, son precisamente ellos los que atraen a millones de visitantes. Lo que antes se despreciaba se ha convertido en la imagen de la ciudad.
Das Erste, was die meisten Touristen in:
The first thing most tourists in Barcelona do is visit the Sagrada Familia. What few people know is that Catalan Modernisme wasn't the work of a single genius. It was a whole movement that transformed the city between 1888 and 1911, and it was architects like Domènech i Montaner or Puig i Cadafalch who left some of its most impressive jewels.

The Palau de la Música Catalana, for example, is probably the building where you can best see what Modernisme was aiming for: combining architecture, sculpture, glass and ceramics in a single work. Anyone going in for the first time has no idea how bright the hall is, thanks to an enormous skylight of coloured glass.

The curious thing is that for decades these buildings were considered "tasteless". It was only from the seventies onwards that people began to appreciate them again. Today, by contrast, it's precisely these buildings that attract millions of visitors. What was once despised has become the city's emblem.

Pocas tecnologías han avanzado tan rápid:
Pocas tecnologías han avanzado tan rápido como la inteligencia artificial. En apenas unos años, los sistemas han pasado de reconocer imágenes a redactar textos, diagnosticar enfermedades o componer música. Si bien estos avances abren posibilidades enormes, también plantean preguntas que todavía no sabemos responder.

Por muy precisos que sean los algoritmos, aprenden de datos creados por personas, con todos nuestros prejuicios. De ahí que algunos sistemas de selección de personal hayan discriminado a mujeres o a candidatos de ciertos barrios sin que nadie lo programara de forma consciente. Y eso que sus creadores pretendían precisamente lo contrario: decisiones más objetivas.

Aun reconociendo estos riesgos, sería un error frenar la investigación. Lo que hace falta es una regulación tan clara que las empresas no puedan esconderse detrás de la «caja negra» de sus algoritmos. Por mucho que nos fascine la tecnología, las decisiones que afectan a personas deberían seguir teniendo, en último término, un responsable humano.
Nur wenige Technologien haben sich so sc:
Few technologies have advanced as quickly as artificial intelligence. In just a few years, systems have gone from recognising images to writing texts, diagnosing diseases or composing music. Although these advances open up enormous possibilities, they also raise questions we don't yet know how to answer.

However precise algorithms may be, they learn from data created by people, with all our prejudices. Hence some recruitment systems have discriminated against women or candidates from certain neighbourhoods without anyone consciously programming them to do so. And that despite their creators intending exactly the opposite: more objective decisions.

Even acknowledging these risks, it would be a mistake to slow down research. What's needed is regulation so clear that companies can't hide behind the "black box" of their algorithms. However much technology fascinates us, decisions that affect people should ultimately still have a human being responsible for them.

Wir leben im Zeitalter der permanenten A:
We live in the age of permanent distraction. A few seconds without stimulation are enough for us to pull our phones out of our pockets. That said: what do we lose when we abolish boredom completely?

As far as creativity is concerned, numerous studies agree that moments of idleness encourage new ideas to emerge. One experiment is worth highlighting, in which a group that had done a monotonous task afterwards found more original solutions than another group that hadn't been bored. That's why some experts speak of boredom as the "engine" of thought.

Having said that, it's not about idealising it. However much it encourages reflection, chronic boredom can turn into apathy. So it seems sensible to win back small spaces of silence: a journey without headphones, a wait without a screen. Perhaps, paradoxically, that's exactly where the best ideas begin.

In Spain many people who work in offices eat out. A very popular option is the “menú del día”. For a fixed price – usually between 12 and 16 euros – you get a starter, a main course, dessert or coffee, bread and a drink.

The starters are often salads, soups or vegetables. As a main course there's meat or fish. In Barcelona, for example, black rice or butifarra (sausage) with beans is typical.

Lunch is the main meal of the day and people don't eat fast: a business lunch can last two hours. That's why dinner is lighter and very late, at nine or ten in the evening.

Lieber Leser: Wenn Sie gerade in ein Hau:
Dear reader: if you've just moved into a building in Barcelona, congratulations. You're about to discover living together with neighbours in its purest form. Allow me a few tips from someone who has lived on the same landing for thirty years.

Firstly: don't you dare greet anyone in the lift with more than a mumbled "bon dia". Telling your life story between the second and fifth floors is extremely rude; that's what residents' meetings are for, which, as everyone knows, are the neighbours' favourite activity. How many happy hours you'll spend arguing about whether the entrance hall should be painted beige or light beige!

Secondly: if your upstairs neighbour decides to move the furniture around at two in the morning, don't complain. He's surely looking for inspiration. Would you really be so selfish as to clip an artist's wings? And finally: if someone asks you for salt, give it to them. You'll never get it back, but you'll gain something far more valuable: a topic of conversation for the next ten years.

Es gab eine Zeit, in der der Sprichworts:
There was a time when the stock of proverbs was a pocket encyclopaedia. Those who couldn't read knew instead that "in April, a thousand rains" and that "the early bird catches the worm". Proverbs condensed centuries of rural experience into easy-to-remember sentences, often rhyming.

Today, by contrast, many young people barely know a dozen. No wonder: a large number of proverbs allude to a rural world that no longer exists. What sense does "raise ravens and they'll peck your eyes out" make to someone who has never seen a raven in their life? Even so, it would be rash to declare them dead. Rather, they're transforming: people quote them ironically, shorten them ("ojos que no ven …") or reinvent them on social media, where "better late than never" sits next to "better a meme than never".

In the end, proverbs aren't disappearing; they're shedding their skin. And perhaps that's their greatest lesson: from saying to doing is a long way, but from proverb to meme is just a click.

La librería de don Esteve cerraba a las:
La librería de don Esteve cerraba a las ocho, pero aquella noche, como tantas otras, las luces seguían encendidas pasadas las diez. Desde la acera de enfrente se le veía, encorvado sobre el mostrador, anotando en un cuaderno de tapas negras lo que nadie le había pedido que anotara: los títulos que no había vendido.

Decían en el barrio que la tienda no sobreviviría al invierno. Lo decían con esa mezcla de pena y alivio con que se habla de lo inevitable. Él, en cambio, abría cada mañana a las nueve en punto, pasara lo que pasara, como si la puntualidad pudiera {conjurar|ward off} el final. Comoquiera que fuese, nadie se atrevía a preguntarle.

Una tarde de enero entró una niña con un billete arrugado en la mano. Quería un libro de piratas, dijo, uno que tuviera mapa. Don Esteve tardó en contestar. Luego subió la escalera de madera, rebuscó en la última estantería y bajó con un volumen descolorido. —Este era mío —dijo—. Tiene mapa y, si lo lees bien, también tesoro. La niña no entendió, pero sonrió. Él no le cobró. Aquella noche, por primera vez en meses, apagó las luces a las ocho.
Don Esteves Buchhandlung schloss um acht:
Don Esteve's bookshop closed at eight, but that night, like so many others, the lights were still on after ten. From the pavement opposite you could see him, hunched over the counter, writing down in a black-covered notebook what nobody had asked him to write down: the titles he hadn't sold.

People in the neighbourhood said the shop wouldn't survive the winter. They said it with that mixture of sorrow and relief with which one speaks of the inevitable. He, on the other hand, opened every morning at nine o'clock sharp, whatever happened, as if punctuality could ward off the end. Be that as it may, nobody dared to ask him.

One January afternoon a girl came in with a crumpled banknote in her hand. She wanted a pirate book, she said, one with a map. Don Esteve took a while to answer. Then he climbed the wooden ladder, rummaged on the top shelf and came down with a faded volume. "This was mine," he said. "It has a map and, if you read it carefully, treasure too." The girl didn't understand, but she smiled. He didn't charge her. That night, for the first time in months, he switched off the lights at eight.

Querido Jonas del primer día:\n\nAhora m:
Querido Jonas del primer día:

Ahora mismo estás en el aeropuerto del Prat, repitiendo en voz baja «Me llamo Jonas, soy alemán». Dentro de un rato te perderás en el metro y pensarás que nunca entenderás a nadie. Déjame decirte algo: lo entenderás. No de golpe, sino poco a poco, como quien sube una montaña sin mirar demasiado hacia arriba.

Vas a meter la pata muchas veces. Dirás «estoy embarazado» cuando quieras decir que te da vergüenza, y la cajera del súper se reirá contigo, no de ti. Aprenderás que «ahora» no significa ahora, que se cena a las diez y que una caña nunca es solo una caña. Te costará distinguir el indefinido del imperfecto, y años después te sorprenderás usando un subjuntivo sin pensarlo.

Si pudiera darte un solo consejo, sería este: no esperes a hablar perfecto para hablar. Pase lo que pase, sigue preguntando, sigue equivocándote, sigue escuchando. Dicho de otro modo: el idioma no se aprende; se vive.

Un abrazo del Jonas que, por fin, sueña en español.
Lieber Jonas vom ersten Tag,\n\ngerade s:
Dear Jonas of the first day,

Right now you're at El Prat airport, quietly repeating "Me llamo Jonas, soy alemán". In a little while you'll get lost in the metro and think you'll never understand anyone. Let me tell you something: you will understand. Not all at once, but little by little, like someone climbing a mountain without looking up too often.

You'll put your foot in it many times. You'll say "estoy embarazado" when you want to say you're embarrassed, and the cashier at the supermarket will laugh with you, not at you. You'll learn that "ahora" doesn't mean now, that people have dinner at ten and that a caña is never just a caña. You'll find it hard to tell the preterite from the imperfect, and years later you'll catch yourself using a subjunctive without thinking.

If I could give you just one piece of advice, it would be this: don't wait until you speak perfectly before you speak. Whatever happens, keep asking, keep making mistakes, keep listening. In other words: you don't learn a language; you live it.

A big hug from the Jonas who, at last, dreams in Spanish.

Barcelona ist eine sehr attraktive Stadt:
Barcelona is a very attractive city for doing business. It has a very important port, an international airport and more than 300 trade fairs and conferences a year, such as the Mobile World Congress.

The city has about 2,500 hours of sunshine a year. That's why many foreigners want to live here. In the centre there are buildings of every style: Gothic ones in the Barri Gòtic and Art Nouveau (modernista) ones in the Eixample, like the Casa Batlló.

Getting around the city is easy because the metro is fast and cheap. But at rush hour there are lots of people and lots of traffic. Many people from Barcelona prefer to cycle: there are more than 300 kilometres of cycle lanes.

Sergi ist 31 Jahre alt und Programmierer:
Sergi is 31 and works as a programmer at a start-up in Barcelona's 22@ district. He works three days at home and two at the office.

“On working-from-home days I get up later than on office days, at eight. Before I start work, I go for a run on the beach. I have a shower, have breakfast and at half past nine I log on. In the morning I'm usually programming and at eleven I meet my team on a video call.

For me, working from home is better than working at the office: I don't waste time on the metro and my hours are more flexible. But it also has disadvantages: sometimes I feel lonely and I work more hours than at the office. That's why I go to the office on Tuesdays and Thursdays: there I see my colleagues and we have lunch together.”

Hace veinte años, la oficina era muy diferente. Casi todos los empleados trabajaban en la empresa de nueve a seis. Cada persona tenía su propio {escritorio|desk} y el jefe estaba en un despacho cerrado. Las reuniones eran siempre {presenciales|in person} y la gente usaba mucho el teléfono fijo.

Ahora las cosas han cambiado. En muchas empresas de Barcelona los equipos trabajan en espacios abiertos y {compartidos|shared}. La mayoría de los trabajadores tiene horarios flexibles y más de la mitad teletrabaja uno o dos días a la semana.

Vor zwanzig Jahren war das Büro ganz and:
Twenty years ago the office was very different. Almost all employees worked at the company from nine to six. Each person had their own desk and the boss sat in a closed office. Meetings were always in person and people used the landline a lot.

Now things have changed. In many companies in Barcelona teams work in open, shared spaces. Most employees have flexible hours and more than half work from home one or two days a week.

But not everything is better: some people find it hard to switch off and few have a suitable workspace at home. That's why many companies are looking for a balance: you have to be at the office some days, but you can also work from home.
